source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 10: sin(a - b) by the cross product of two unit vectors (book p.283). The book prints + instead of - on the right side. Proof, no key answer.

blocks.explanation:
A trigonometric identity proved with vectors.
We must find one cross product in two ways and compare.
Plan: two unit vectors at angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\); the definition gives \(\sin(\alpha - \beta)\), the determinant gives the right side.
steps:
Given: angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (take \(\alpha > \beta\)).
To prove: \(\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\).
Method: As in Example 17: in the \(xy\)-plane draw unit vectors \(\underline{OA}\) and \(\underline{OB}\) making angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with the \(x\)-axis. The angle between them is \(\alpha - \beta\).

Write the two unit vectors
\[\underline{OA} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\]
\[\underline{OB} = \cos\beta\,\underline{i} + \sin\beta\,\underline{j}\]
Why: A unit vector at angle \(\alpha\) to the \(x\)-axis has components \(\cos\alpha\) and \(\sin\alpha\); its length is \(\sqrt{\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha} = 1\).

Cross product from the definition
\[\underline{OB} \times \underline{OA} = (1)(1)\sin(\alpha - \beta)\,\underline{k}\]
\[= \sin(\alpha - \beta)\,\underline{k} \quad (1)\]
Why: Both lengths are 1, the angle from \(\underline{OB}\) to \(\underline{OA}\) is \(\alpha - \beta\), and turning from \(\underline{OB}\) to \(\underline{OA}\) is counter-clockwise, so the right hand rule gives \(+\underline{k}\).

The same cross product from the determinant
\[\underline{OB} \times \underline{OA} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ \cos\beta & \sin\beta & 0 \\ \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \underline{i}(0) - \underline{j}(0)\]
\[+ \underline{k}(\cos\beta\sin\alpha - \sin\beta\cos\alpha)\]
\[= (\sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\,\underline{k} \quad (2)\]
Why: Both vectors have \(\underline{k}\)-component 0, so the \(\underline{i}\) and \(\underline{j}\) minors are 0.

Compare (1) and (2)
\[\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: Two expressions of the same vector are equal, so their \(\underline{k}\)-components are equal.

Check with numbers
\[\alpha = 90^{\circ},\ \beta = 30^{\circ}:\ \sin 60^{\circ} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
\[(1)\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - (0)\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
Why: Both sides give \(\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). With the printed \(+\) sign, \(\alpha = \beta = 45^{\circ}\) would give \(\sin 0 = 1\), which is false.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\). This is wrong: the right side with \(+\) is \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\). The correct identity is \(\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\), which is what the cross product proves.
